enonce_markdown: A single fixed pulley, fixed to a beam above a well, is used to raise a bucket of water by pulling on a rope that passes over it. What is the advantage of using this pulley?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A single fixed pulley has a velocity ratio of $1$: the effort moves the same distance as the load, and (ignoring friction) the effort equals the load. Its only advantage is to change the direction of the force. Machines never give out more energy than is put in.

### Solution

With one fixed pulley the number of rope sections supporting the load is $1$, so $\mathrm{VR} = 1$. The effort is not smaller than the load (it is actually larger, because of friction and the weight of the rope), and the effort moves the same distance as the load. The advantage is that the user can **pull downwards**, using their own weight, instead of lifting upwards. **Answer: a.**

choix.texte: It changes the direction of the effort, so the user can pull downwards.
It makes the effort half of the weight of the bucket.
It makes the effort move a shorter distance than the bucket.
It gives out more energy than is put in.

enonce_markdown: A block-and-tackle pulley system has $5$ sections of rope supporting the lower (movable) block and the load. The load is raised by $0.40\,\mathrm{m}$. The distance moved by the effort is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The velocity ratio of a pulley system equals the number of rope sections supporting the movable block: $\mathrm{VR} = n$. Also $\mathrm{VR} = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by effort}}{\text{distance moved by load}}$.

### Solution

$\mathrm{VR} = 5$.

Distance moved by the effort $= \mathrm{VR} \times \text{distance moved by the load} = 5 \times 0.40 = 2.0\,\mathrm{m}$.

$0.08\,\mathrm{m}$ comes from dividing instead of multiplying; $0.40\,\mathrm{m}$ assumes the effort and load move the same distance (as for a single fixed pulley); $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ is the velocity ratio taken as a distance. **Answer: c.**

enonce_markdown: A pulley system with a velocity ratio of $3$ is used to lift a load of $600\,\mathrm{N}$. An effort of $250\,\mathrm{N}$ is needed. The efficiency of the system is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

$\text{Mechanical advantage } \mathrm{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$ and $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\mathrm{MA}}{\mathrm{VR}} \times 100\,\%$ (which is also $\dfrac{\text{work output}}{\text{work input}} \times 100\,\%$).

### Solution

$\mathrm{MA} = \dfrac{600}{250} = 2.4$.

$\text{Efficiency} = \dfrac{2.4}{3} \times 100\,\% = 80\,\%$.

$41.7\,\%$ comes from effort $\div$ load; $125\,\%$ comes from inverting $\mathrm{MA}/\mathrm{VR}$ (an efficiency above $100\,\%$ is impossible); $240\,\%$ is the mechanical advantage written as a percentage. **Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown: A block-and-tackle system with a velocity ratio of $4$ and an efficiency of $75\,\%$ is used to raise a load of $900\,\mathrm{N}$ through a height of $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$. The work done by the effort is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Work done $= \text{force} \times \text{distance moved in the direction of the force}$. $\text{Efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{work output}}{\text{work input}}$, so $\text{work input} = \dfrac{\text{work output}}{\text{efficiency}}$ (the effort does more work than is usefully delivered to the load).

### Solution

Useful work output (on the load): $W_{\text{out}} = 900 \times 2.0 = 1800\,\mathrm{J}$.

Work input (by the effort): $W_{\text{in}} = \dfrac{1800}{0.75} = 2400\,\mathrm{J}$.

Check using forces and distances: $\mathrm{MA} = 4 \times 0.75 = 3$, so effort $= \dfrac{900}{3} = 300\,\mathrm{N}$; effort distance $= 4 \times 2.0 = 8.0\,\mathrm{m}$; $W_{\text{in}} = 300 \times 8.0 = 2400\,\mathrm{J}$.

$1800\,\mathrm{J}$ is the work done on the load; $1350\,\mathrm{J}$ multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing; $1200\,\mathrm{J}$ multiplies the effort by the velocity ratio instead of by the effort distance. **Answer: d.**

enonce_markdown:
A builder in Bamenda uses a block-and-tackle with $4$ rope sections supporting the lower block to raise a bag of cement of mass $40\,\mathrm{kg}$ through a height of $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$. He pulls the free end of the rope with a steady effort of $125\,\mathrm{N}$. (Take $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.)

(a) State the velocity ratio of the system.

(b) Calculate the weight of the bag, the mechanical advantage and the efficiency of the system.

(c) Calculate the distance moved by the effort.

(d) Calculate the work done by the effort, the useful work done on the bag, and the energy wasted. Say where the wasted energy goes.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

$\mathrm{VR} = $ number of rope sections supporting the lower block; $\mathrm{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$; $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\mathrm{MA}}{\mathrm{VR}} \times 100\,\%$; work done $= \text{force} \times \text{distance}$.

### Solution

(a) $\mathrm{VR} = 4$ (the number of rope sections supporting the lower block).

(b) Weight $= mg = 40 \times 10 = 400\,\mathrm{N}$.

$\mathrm{MA} = \dfrac{400}{125} = 3.2$.

$\text{Efficiency} = \dfrac{3.2}{4} \times 100\,\% = 80\,\%$.

(c) Distance moved by the effort $= \mathrm{VR} \times 3.0 = 4 \times 3.0 = 12\,\mathrm{m}$.

(d) Work done by the effort: $125 \times 12 = 1500\,\mathrm{J}$.

Useful work on the bag: $400 \times 3.0 = 1200\,\mathrm{J}$.

Energy wasted: $1500 - 1200 = 300\,\mathrm{J}$. Check: $\dfrac{1200}{1500} \times 100\,\% = 80\,\%$, the same efficiency as in (b).

The wasted energy is transferred as heat by friction in the pulley axles and between the rope and the pulleys, and it also raises the weight of the lower block and rope.

enonce_markdown:
A pulley system with $4$ rope sections supporting the lower block is tested with different loads. The effort $E$ needed to raise each load steadily is:

| Load $L/\mathrm{N}$ | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Effort $E/\mathrm{N}$ | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 |

(a) State the velocity ratio of the system.

(b) For each load, calculate the mechanical advantage and the efficiency of the system.

(c) Describe how the efficiency changes as the load increases, and explain why.

(d) A graph of $E$ (vertical axis) against $L$ (horizontal axis) is a straight line. Find its gradient and its intercept on the vertical axis, and state what the intercept represents.

(e) Use the straight line to find the effort needed for a load of $200\,\mathrm{N}$, and the efficiency at this load.

(f) Explain why the efficiency of a real pulley system can never reach $100\,\%$.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

$\mathrm{VR} = n$ (rope sections supporting the lower block); $\mathrm{MA} = \dfrac{L}{E}$; $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\mathrm{MA}}{\mathrm{VR}} \times 100\,\%$. For a straight line $y = mx + c$, the gradient is $\dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ and the intercept $c$ is the value of $y$ when $x = 0$.

### Solution

(a) $\mathrm{VR} = 4$.

(b)

| Load $L/\mathrm{N}$ | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{MA} = L/E$ | 2.0 | 2.7 | 3.0 | 3.2 |
| Efficiency $= \dfrac{\mathrm{MA}}{4} \times 100\,\%$ | $50\,\%$ | $66.7\,\%$ | $75\,\%$ | $80\,\%$ |

(c) The efficiency increases as the load increases. The effort has to overcome the fixed losses (the weight of the lower block, and friction in the pulleys) in addition to the load; these losses are almost the same for every load, so they are a smaller fraction of the total work done when the load is large.

(d) Gradient $= \dfrac{25 - 10}{80 - 20} = \dfrac{15}{60} = 0.25 = \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{VR}}$.

Intercept: $E = 10 - 0.25 \times 20 = 5\,\mathrm{N}$. This is the effort needed to overcome the weight of the lower block and the friction when the load is (almost) zero.

The line is $E = 0.25L + 5$.

(e) For $L = 200\,\mathrm{N}$: $E = 0.25 \times 200 + 5 = 55\,\mathrm{N}$.

$\mathrm{MA} = \dfrac{200}{55} = 3.64$, so efficiency $= \dfrac{3.64}{4} \times 100\,\% = 90.9\,\%$.

(f) Friction in the pulleys and the weight of the moving lower block and rope mean that part of the work done by the effort is always wasted as heat, so the work output is always less than the work input and the efficiency is less than $100\,\%$. (Even an ideal system would only reach $100\,\%$ when there are no losses.)
